title: Your Mother's Haldi Doodh Is Now a $7 Turmeric Latte
excerpt: As turmeric mentions surge 157 percent on American menus, NRIs are watching their grandmothers' remedies get repackaged — and repriced — as premium wellness trends.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Turmeric mentions on American menus surged 157.1% in nonalcoholic beverages.
  • The global masala chai market exceeded $5.4 billion in 2023.
  • Indian food brands are thriving, with over $5 billion in US and UK at-home consumption.
  • Turmeric lattes symbolize a blend of cultural pride and commercialization for NRIs.
  • Industry analysts predict continued growth for Indian wellness ingredients in the US.

Every NRI has the same story. Your mother forced you to drink haldi doodh when you had a cold. You hated it. You made faces. You poured it down the sink when she wasn't looking. Now the same drink sits under a chalkboard sign at a café in Brooklyn, dusted with cinnamon and served in a ceramic cup for $7. They call it a "golden milk latte." ## The Numbers Don't Lie Turmeric is having a moment that transcends the spice aisle. According to Technomic's MenuMonitor, mentions of turmeric on American menus have surged 157.1 percent in the nonalcoholic beverages category. Cafés from San Francisco's As Quoted to Los Angeles' Cafe Gratitude chain are promoting turmeric lattes not as exotic curiosity but as functional wellness drinks — anti-inflammatory, antioxidant-rich, gut-friendly. The broader masala chai market tells a similar story. According to Verified Market Research, the global masala chai market exceeded $5.4 billion in 2023 and could approach $10 billion by 2031. TikTok has been a major accelerant, with chai-making videos routinely crossing half a million views. But social media only amplified what was already building: a convergence of café culture, globalization, and health consciousness that has put Indian beverages squarely in the mainstream. ## Repackaged Wisdom An Indian woman named Smidha, now living in Australia, captured the diaspora sentiment perfectly in an Instagram post that went viral across NRI communities. "Mom roz haldi doodh banati thi jo hum peene se bhagte the," she wrote. "Same ingredients, same warmth — we just called it gross." Her observation cut deeper than turmeric. She pointed to handwoven dupattas selling for $200 in Australian boutiques and Ayurvedic practices rebranded as "holistic wellness" at premium spas. "We don't lose our culture to the West," she concluded. "We just stop seeing the value in it first." This dynamic — Indian traditions dismissed at home, then embraced abroad at a markup — is one of the defining ironies of diaspora life. Ghee was "unhealthy" until wellness influencers made it a superfood. Yoga was "old people stuff" until it became a $12-billion American industry. And now the turmeric your grandmother swore by is the star ingredient at juice bars from Portland to Miami. ## Beyond the Latte The trend extends well beyond beverages. Indian food brands are capitalizing on the mainstreaming of Indian ingredients. Truly Indian, backed by ADF Foods, recently earned two finalist placements in the 2026 NEXTY Awards — the natural products industry's Oscars — for its Tikka Masala Naan and Crispy Chili Mango Chutney. The brand has expanded to over 1,300 US stores since its 2024 launch. Meanwhile, Gymkhana Fine Foods, born from London's two-Michelin-starred Gymkhana restaurant, just launched its simmer sauces in Whole Foods nationwide with $8.5 million in venture backing. Indian food now accounts for more than $5 billion in at-home consumption across the US and UK. Even in the restaurant world, Indian ingredients are no longer exotic add-ons. Vadouvan, an Indian curry blend, has seen 71.4 percent growth on independent restaurant menus, according to Technomic. Chains like Sweetgreen and Bahama Breeze have incorporated curry into their offerings. ## The Diaspora Reckoning For NRIs, the turmeric latte phenomenon prompts a complicated mix of pride and exasperation. Pride that the world is finally catching up to what Indian kitchens have known for centuries. Exasperation that it took a rebrand, a markup, and a ceramic cup to get there. But there is a more productive way to read the trend. Every turmeric latte sold is an entry point — a first step toward biryani, toward dal makhani, toward the full depth of a cuisine that has spent centuries perfecting the relationship between spice and health. The golden milk latte isn't an appropriation. It's an invitation. And your mother knew about it first. ## What's Next Industry analysts expect Indian wellness ingredients — turmeric, ashwagandha, moringa, and amla — to continue growing in the American functional food and beverage space. The key question for Indian brands is whether they can own this category or whether Western wellness companies will continue to repackage Indian knowledge without Indian ownership. Brands like Truly Indian and Gymkhana, with their direct connections to Indian culinary heritage, are positioned to lead — if they move fast enough.
